item.title: Editing Enzymes with Multiscale Metal-Based Components.
item.abstract: Enzymes are powerful natural catalysts distinguished by high efficiency and selectivity. The use of enzymes in the chemical industry can theoretically enable numerous efficient and sustainable reaction pathways. Nevertheless, the application of enzymes is hindered by their narrow catalytic repertoire. Enzymes are readily deactivated under nonnatural environments, and their reaction types are limited. Developing enzymes with new catalytic functions has been a longstanding challenge in the field of biocatalysis. Strategies such as directed evolution and de novo protein design have been very successful in designing new enzymes. However, as both approaches rely on the engineering of amino acid sequences of proteins, they remain constrained and cannot fully meet the growing demand for non-natural biocatalysis. Incorporating abiotic components with enzymes is a powerful tool for editing enzymes to render new catalytic capabilities. Metal-based components possess a broad catalytic repertoire, structural stability, and multifunctionality, making them promising building blocks for enzyme editing. This Account summarizes our contributions over the past decade in editing enzyme catalysts with metal-based components as a scale-dependent evolution, from nanoscale environmental modulation to atom-scale active site redefinition, illustrating how enzyme editing with metal-based components can systematically address non-natural catalytic challenges. A conceptual framework in which enzymes are edited with metal-based components across scales from the nanometer to the atomic dimension is introduced, establishing a logical basis for integrating biocatalysis with abiotic reactivity. At the nanoscale, enzymes are encapsulated in metal-based frameworks to improve the configuration stability, enabling catalysis under non-native and harsh conditions. The robustness of enzymes under extreme pH, high temperature, and organic solvent can be largely enhanced through the regulation of metal-based frameworks. At the sub-nanoscale, metal clusters are embedded within enzyme scaffolds to construct enzyme-metal hybrid catalysts. By integration of enzymatic and chemical catalysis, new non-natural catalytic processes can be established. At the atomic scale, metal atoms are incorporated into the enzyme catalytic pocket, creating new hybrid active sites. The hybrid active site endows an enzyme with capabilities to drive new-to-nature reactions, unlocking an expanded enzyme catalytic space. This work provides a unifying conceptual framework that clarifies how metal-based components can be strategically employed to reprogram enzyme stability, functionality, and reactivity. We hope that the strategies and concepts discussed herein offer comprehensive design principles for biohybrid catalysts and establish a foundation for reprogramming enzymatic function beyond evolutionary limitations.

item.title: Genome editing beyond transgenes: DNA-free technologies in crop improvement.
item.abstract: Conventional and transgenic approaches to crop improvement are increasingly constrained by biosafety concerns, stringent regulatory frameworks, and limited public acceptance, necessitating new precision breeding methods. DNA-free genome editing using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach has emerged as a transformative approach that enables precise, targeted genetic modifications without the stable integration of a foreign gene (transgene). This strategy transiently introduces CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, or in vitro transcribed mRNA, into plant cells. This review focuses primarily on CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing and its applications in crop improvement. After targeted genome cleavage, the editing elements are rapidly degraded, leaving only the desired genomic modification and resulting in plants indistinguishable from those developed through conventional breeding. To achieve targeted, DNA-free genome editing, researchers have developed numerous molecular platforms and delivery systems, such as protoplast transfection, biolistic bombardment, nanoparticle-based systems, and emerging pollen- and meristem-targeted systems, for major crop species. Researchers have successfully enhanced several notable traits, including disease and pest resistance, nutritional quality, abiotic stress tolerance, and agronomic performance, in cereals, vegetables, oilseeds, and perennial crops. Recent advancements, including base editing, prime editing, and multiplex gene editing, are further expanding the precision, efficiency, and scope of DNA-free genome editing. Overall, CRISPR/Cas-mediated DNA-free genome editing offers a route to crop improvement that avoids stable transgene integration, though its wider deployment depends on progress in regeneration, molecular validation, and regulatory convergence.

item.title: Advances and applications of engineered protein therapeutics and their role in precision medicine.
item.abstract: Proteins are a vital class of biomolecules. They play essential roles in biological processes, including building cellular structures, forming cellular channels and receptors, catalyzing biological reactions, transporting molecules, and contributing to immune defense mechanisms. Advances in protein engineering have enabled the genetic modification of naturally occurring proteins, using recombinant deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) technology, leading to the development of therapeutic proteins with enhanced specificity, stability, and clinical performance. Despite the rapid growth of engineered biologics, a comprehensive understanding of how these innovations intersect with precision medicine remains limited. This review addresses this gap by summarizing the major contemporary approaches used in therapeutic protein engineering, including directed evolution, rational design, and de novo protein design, and by analyzing their roles in enabling patient-tailored interventions. It provides an integrated overview of the clinical applications of engineered therapeutic proteins across key medical fields, supported by a list of U.S. Food and Drug Administration- and European Medicines Agency-approved protein therapeutics from 2020 to 2025. The review further provides a comparative perspective on major protein engineering strategies, highlighting their relative advantages and limitations, while examining differences in clinical translation across major disease areas. By combining technological advances with disease-specific applications, this review offers a perspective that has not been fully developed in the literature. Finally, the review discusses the current challenges affecting the implementation of precision medicine, including immunogenicity, regulatory constraints, and ethical considerations, and outlines future directions, such as artificial intelligence-guided protein design, targeted protein degradation, and personalized vaccine development. Collectively, these insights highlight the expanding role of engineered proteins in shaping the next-generation of precision therapeutics and emphasize the growing importance of integrating multidisciplinary approaches to advance therapeutic innovation in modern clinical practice.

item.title: Efficient genome editing in ASC-derived porcine lung organoids via GFP-guided enrichment.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adult stem cell-derived organoids are invaluable tools for disease modeling and translational medicine owing to their tissue-specific correspondence. However, their complex three-dimensional structure and low genome-editing efficiency have posed significant challenges for functional genetic studies. To address these limitations, this study aimed to establish porcine lung organoid (PLOs) and to develop a robust, high-efficiency genome-editing platform by leveraging the high physiological and anatomical similarity between pigs and humans.
METHODS: PLOs were derived from lung tissues and characterized by immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry analysis. To enhance genome-editing efficiency using CRISPR/Cas9 and prime editing, a GFP-guided enrichment strategy was used by co-targeting a GFP transgene and endogenous loci, followed by the selection of GFP-negative organoids. Clonal expansion from single organoids was performed to generate genetically homogenous lines. Genetic modifications were validated through cDNA sequencing and western blot analysis. Structural integrity was assessed using AlphaFold2 modeling, and functional changes were evaluated using the forskolin-induced swelling assay.
RESULTS: The established PLOs exhibited sustained self-renewal capacity and expression of surfactant protein C alongside both proximal epithelial and mesenchymal markers, reflecting a composite lung organoid identity. GFP-guided enrichment significantly enriched edited cells; the mutation ratio in the GFP-negative group was significantly higher than that in the GFP-positive group. This system successfully generated fully gene-edited clones with high genetic homogeneity, and effectively enriched for precisely edited organoids, even when applying complex modalities such as prime editing.
CONCLUSIONS: The PLOs and genome-editing platform developed in this study provide a powerful resource for translational medicine. By enabling precise genetic manipulation in a model that closely mimics human lung physiology, this system offers an essential platform for recapitulating human lung pathologies, studying zoonotic infectious diseases, and validating the efficacy of gene therapies.

item.title: A base-editing and auxotrophic selection platform for linking epigenetic regulators to silent biosynthetic gene clusters in Aspergillus nidulans.
item.abstract: Filamentous fungi harbor numerous silent biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), representing an underexplored reservoir of natural products. Chemical inhibition of epigenetic regulators is an effective strategy for activating silent BGCs, but it often lacks specificity and cannot readily link activated clusters to their cognate regulators. Here, we developed a coupled cytosine base editing and auxotrophic selection platform in Aspergillus nidulans to systematically identify epigenetic regulators of silent gene clusters. An sgRNA library targeting 24 core epigenetic regulators was introduced, together with a cytosine base editor, into 21 pyrG-based PKS reporter strains, enabling growth-based selection and direct sgRNA recovery by Sanger sequencing. This screen identified five regulator-cluster activation pairs, including known interactions and two previously uncharacterized mechanisms. Specifically, KdmB represses the AN7084 gene cluster by erasing promoter H3K4me3, whereas Kmt5 silences the cichorine core pks gene through H4K20me3 deposition. This scalable platform enables rapid matching of silent BGCs with their epigenetic regulators and advances chromatin-guided fungal genome mining.

item.title: DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel reprograms the immuno-oxidative microenvironment to support stem cell-based cartilage repair in osteoarthritis.
item.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent degenerative joint disease, and stem cell therapy is often limited by a hostile joint microenvironment. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) and damage-associated cell-free DNA (cfDNA) cooperatively drive innate immune activation, inflammatory macrophage polarization, and chondrogenic instability, forming an immuno-oxidative barrier to cartilage repair. Here, we developed a bioactive DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel (MNKB/HA) to remodel this niche and enhance BMSC-mediated cartilage repair. MNKB/HA integrates Mn3O4 nanozymes with Kartogenin (KGN)-engineered bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) in an injectable hyaluronic acid matrix. Mn3O4 exhibited SOD- and CAT-like activities, scavenging O2·-, H2O2, and ·OH, while efficiently adsorbing cfDNA and CpG-ODN to suppress TLR9/MyD88 signaling and M1 polarization and promote M2 polarization. In vitro, 10 μg/mL Mn3O4 was cytocompatible, protected BMSCs and chondrocytes from H2O2-induced apoptosis, and reshaped inflammatory secretion, with IL-10 increased 8.3-fold and TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β reduced. KGN stabilized the chondrogenic phenotype (SOX9, COL Ⅱ, ACAN), while its combination with Mn3O4 synergistically enhanced chondrogenic stability under oxidative/inflammatory stress. In rat OA, intra-articular MNKB/HA reduced OARSI scores, restored COL II and ACAN, decreased MMP13, improved subchondral bone microarchitecture, and attenuated synovitis and osteophytes. MNKB/HA also reduced synovial cfDNA, weakened TLR9 signaling, promoted M2 polarization, and showed intra-articular retention for at least 10 days without notable systemic toxicity. Thus, MNKB/HA remodels the immuno-oxidative niche through synergistic ROS scavenging and cfDNA adsorption, providing a strategy for stem cell-mediated cartilage repair in OA.

item.title: Graphene oxide-induced multiple iPSC spheroid formation for enhanced production of angiogenic exosomes accelerating tissue regeneration.
item.abstract: Exosome-based therapeutics have emerged as a promising cell-free strategy for tissue regeneration by coordinating angiogenesis and tissue repair. Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived exosomes are particularly attractive because of their regenerative potential and scalability; however, the reproducible and scalable production of functionally potent exosomes remains a major barrier to clinical translation. Here, we developed a graphene oxide (GO)-mediated nanoengineering strategy to establish a multi-spheroid platform that simultaneously regulates spheroid architecture, enhances exosome production, and improves angiogenic functionality in both iPSC spheroids and iPSC-derived vascular endothelial cell (vEC) spheroids. GO reproducibly reorganized cellular aggregation from a single dominant spheroid into multiple uniformly sized spheroids per well and increased exosome production while preserving characteristic vesicle properties. GO-engineered iPSC spheroid-derived exosomes exhibited distinct angiogenesis-related miRNA profiles and significantly enhanced endothelial cell migration and capillary-like network formation in vitro. Extending this strategy to iPSC-vEC spheroids further enhanced endothelial differentiation and generated lineage-specific exosomes with greater pro-angiogenic activity. In a rat full-thickness skin wound model, GO-engineered spheroid-derived exosomes accelerated wound closure and promoted vascularized skin regeneration. Collectively, these findings establish GO-mediated spheroid nanoengineering as a reproducible and potentially scalable strategy for producing therapeutically potent exosomes. By integrating controlled spheroid formation, enhanced exosome productivity, preserved vesicle characteristics, and improved angiogenic efficacy, this platform provides a practical framework for standardized exosome manufacturing and supports its future clinical translation toward vascular regenerative therapies.

item.title: Size-Dependent Zinc Delivery and Nanozyme-Mediated Stress Alleviation by ZnO Nanoparticles in Zinc-Deficient Tomato.
item.abstract: Zinc (Zn) deficiency severely limits plant growth and yield, highlighting the need for strategies to improve Zn nutrition. Here, Zn oxide nanoparticles (nZnOs) of two sizes (∼8 nm and ∼45 nm, 100 mg·L-1) were evaluated as seed priming agents in tomato grown under Zn-deficient conditions. Both nanoparticle sizes were internalized into embryonic tissues and showed distinct intracellular localization. While 45 nm nZnO and bulk Zn disturbed seed nutrient homeostasis, 8 nm nZnO increased seed Zn content more efficiently, with milder effects on other nutrients. Across developmental stages, nZnO priming improved Zn supply and nutrient distribution more effectively than bulk Zn. At the vegetative stage, 45 nm nZnO enhanced overall biomass, whereas 8 nm nZnO promoted root-specific growth under Zn deficiency. nZnO priming increased root Zn accumulation, particularly with 8 nm nZnO, and alleviated Zn deficiency-induced nonspecific metal accumulation. Zn deficiency-induced disturbances in redox and nitrosative balance were reversed by nZnO priming, accompanied by reduced RNA nitration and a shift toward a catalase-dominated hydrogen peroxide detoxification system. Both nanoparticle sizes exhibited peroxidase-like activity in cell-free assays, indicating nanozyme potential; however, this activity did not translate directly to the in planta responses. Under Zn deficiency, nZnO priming suppressed stress-related metabolic pathways in leaves, while enhancing amino acid, polyamine, and structural carbohydrate metabolism in roots. Zn deficiency-induced transcriptional repression, particularly in leaves, was partially restored, with affected genes enriched in stress-, phytohormone-, and detoxification-related pathways. Overall, size-dependent nZnO seed priming alleviates Zn deficiency in tomato. 45 nm nZnO mainly enhances biomass through improved nutrient homeostasis and redox regulation, while both sizes contribute to restored Zn availability and antioxidant reprogramming under Zn deficiency.

item.title: Optical Control of Therapeutic Synthetic Cells: Controlling Biomolecule Synthesis, Activation, and Communication.
item.abstract: Synthetic cells are emerging as promising platforms that combine cell-free biomolecule synthesis with the programmability of bottom-up engineered compartments. By decoupling biomolecule production from cellular growth and evolutionary constraints, synthetic cells enable the controlled generation of proteins, nucleic acids, peptides, and signaling molecules within defined artificial environments. However, many envisioned biomedical applications require precise regulation over biomolecule synthesis, activation, transport, release, and communication. In this Review, we examine how light can provide spatiotemporal control over synthetic cell functions relevant to future therapeutic applications. We compare external control modalities and review optical strategies that regulate synthetic cell functions across multiple functional layers, including biomolecule synthesis, activation, transport and release, communication, and systems-level integration. Particular emphasis is placed on integrating optical control with cell-free expression systems, RNA-based regulatory platforms, membrane engineering, and emerging synthetic cell architectures. We further discuss challenges associated with system integration, biomolecule complexity, energy management, light delivery, and translation. By classifying optical methodologies according to the functional layers they regulate, we provide a methodology-centered framework for comparing and integrating optical-control strategies toward increasingly sophisticated light-responsive synthetic cell platforms for future therapeutic applications.

item.title: Rational design and synthesis of furan-based Schiff base quinazolin-4-amine hybrids: spectral elucidation, molecular docking, DFT studies, and in silico ADMET-antioxidant study.
item.abstract: In this work, a new series of furan-based quinazoline-4-amine hydrazone (Schiff base) derivatives (4a-h) was rationally designed and synthesized in good yields (84-90%) through a multistep route involving nucleophilic aromatic substitution, Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling, and hydrazone/Schiff base condensation reactions. The synthesized compounds were characterized by FT-IR, 1H NMR, 13C NMR, and ESI-mass spectrometry, which confirmed the proposed structures. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to optimize the molecular geometries and to derive frontier molecular orbital energies, global reactivity descriptors, Mulliken atomic charges, and molecular electrostatic potential (MEP) surfaces, providing insight into the stability, reactivity, and radical-scavenging propensity of the compounds. Molecular docking studies against the Kelch domain of Keap1 (PDB 4L7B), the principal negative regulator of the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response, were carried out using the Schrödinger Suite (Glide, Maestro interface) to explore, in silico, a possible interaction of the derivatives with this target; the docked compounds gave Glide docking scores of -7.325 to -8.603 kcal mol; these results constitute an in silico hypothesis of Keap1 binding that remains to be tested experimentally. Computational ADMET profiling indicated drug-like physicochemical properties overall, with the dimethoxy- and phenolic-substituted analogues 4e and 4h showing the most favourable predicted oral bioavailability (score = 0.55) among the series. The in vitro antioxidant potential of compounds 4a-h was evaluated using the DPPH radical-scavenging assay, giving IC50 values of 85.5 ± 3.7 to 148.1 ± 3.2 µM, compared with 235.2 ± 4.6 µM for the standard antioxidant ascorbic acid; on a molar basis, all eight derivatives were therefore more potent than ascorbic acid in this cell-free assay. Among the series, compounds 4d and 4f displayed the most promising radical-scavenging activity (IC50 = 85.5 and 90.8 µM, respectively), although the global DFT reactivity descriptors did not correlate with the measured activity across the series.

item.title: Repurposed catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors tolcapone and entacapone preferentially suppress aggregation and seeding of P301 mutant tau in human neuronal models.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Pathogenic aggregation and propagation of seed-competent TAU assemblies drive tauopathies. MAPT P301 mutations accelerate aggregation and enhance seed competence, yet pharmacological strategies selectively targeting these pathogenic species remain limited. We investigated whether the clinically approved catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors tolcapone (TOL) and entacapone (ENT) preferentially modulate mutant TAU aggregation and seeding.
EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: TOL and ENT effects on TAU aggregation were evaluated via cell-free assays, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and in silico docking. Functional consequences of compound-modified fibrils were assessed in mutant TAU-expressing SH-SY5Y cells. Translational relevance was examined in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons exposed to pathogenic K18 fibrils, followed by post-seeding compound treatment.
KEY RESULTS: Both compounds dose-dependently inhibited TAU aggregation, exhibiting greater potency, stronger SPR binding affinities, and more favourable computed interaction energies for P301S mutant versus wild-type TAU. Fibrils formed with TOL or ENT induced less downstream TAU oligomerization and phosphorylation in SH-SY5Y cells, with TOL showing superior protection. In hiPSC-derived neurons, post-seeding treatment with either compound decreased fibril-induced, sarkosyl-insoluble, TAU aggregation and phosphorylation without overt cytotoxicity.
CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: TOL and ENT preferentially reduced the aggregation and seeding of pathogenic P301 mutant TAU in the experimental models examined. These findings provide proof-of-concept support for mutation-focused pharmacological approaches and identify catechol scaffolds as starting points for developing more potent and safer TAU-directed compounds. Further studies are required to define the relevant molecular interactions, confirm the neuronal findings across additional hiPSC lines and determine whether effective CNS exposure can be achieved in vivo.

item.title: Diagnostic Performance of cfDNA-Based Liquid Biopsy for Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.abstract: Conventional surveillance tools for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) have limited sensitivity. Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA)-based liquid biopsy is a promising minimally invasive approach; however, its overall diagnostic performance remains unclear. This meta-analysis aimed to comprehensively evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of cfDNA-based liquid biopsy in HCC. Following PRISMA-DTA guidelines, we searched PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science until July 2026. Diagnostic accuracy data were pooled using bivariate random-effects models. Methodological quality was assessed using QUADAS-2 and NOS. A total of 29 studies (4250 HCC patients, 7982 controls) were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity of cfDNA-based testing were 0.82 (95% CI: 0.76-0.86) and 0.91 (95% CI: 0.88-0.93). The area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.93 (95% CI: 0.91-0.96). Subgroup analyses showed higher sensitivity in advanced HCC 0.91 (95% CI: 0.85-0.95) than early HCC 0.77 (95% CI: 0.71-0.83). Methylation profiling yielded relatively higher sensitivity 0.84 (95% CI: 0.77-0.89), whereas fragmentomics showed relatively favorable specificity 0.93 (95% CI: 0.88-0.96). Combining cfDNA-based testing with alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) significantly improved sensitivity compared with cfDNA alone (0.78 vs. 0.65). No significant publication bias was detected (p = 0.83). cfDNA-based liquid biopsy achieves high diagnostic accuracy for HCC. As exploratory observations, methylation-based assays with relatively higher sensitivity may have potential value for screening high-risk populations, while fragmentomics-based assays with relatively favorable specificity may aid differential diagnosis. Combining cfDNA-based liquid biopsy with AFP further improves diagnostic performance, supporting cfDNA as a promising noninvasive tool for HCC detection. Trial Registration: This systematic review was registered on PROSPERO: CRD420261293877 (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/).

item.title: Chitinase biosynthesis and antifungal chitin bioconversion by Streptomyces mutabilis Ssg through statistical optimisation: an agro-industrial waste valorisation approach.
item.abstract: Chitin valorisation through enzymatic bioconversion offers a sustainable route for converting biowastes into value-added bioactive products. In this study, the chitinolytic strain Ssg, showing close phylogenetic affinity with Streptomyces mutabilis, was evaluated for chitinase production in a waste-integrated submerged fermentation system based on crustacean-derived colloidal chitin and supplemented with date seed and orange-peel powders as low-cost co-substrates. The isolate showed a high chitinolytic index of 17.20 ± 0.70. Plackett-Burman screening identified substrate composition and incubation time as key determinants of chitinase production, while Box-Behnken optimisation revealed significant interaction effects and identified the best-performing combination. At 10 g/L date seed powder, 4.08 g/L orange peel powder, and 72 h of incubation, chitinase activity reached 3196 ± 1.73 U/mL, closely matching the predicted value of 3198.01 U/mL. Optimisation increased enzyme production 7.6-fold and reduced fermentation time from 6 days to 72 h. Specific activity also increased from 4870 ± 170 to 13,620 ± 105 U/mg, reflecting stronger chitinolytic performance of the optimised preparation. Both the Optimised Cell-Free Supernatant and the crude chitin hydrolysate exhibited comparable antifungal activity against Aspergillus brasiliensis and Fusarium sp., with a slight advantage for the hydrolysate. The strongest response was observed against Fusarium sp. with the crude chitin hydrolysate, showing an inhibition zone of 24.00 ± 1.00 mm and mycelial growth inhibition of 38.75%. Microscopic observations revealed hyphal deformation and structural disorganisation. Overall, this study establishes a waste-integrated strategy for high-level chitinase production and supports the potential of the Ssg system for chitin bioconversion and biocontrol-oriented applications.

item.title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing.
item.abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.

item.title: Extended Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing for Chromosomal and Monogenic Disorders by Cell-Free DNA Sequencing: A Blinded Comparison With Amniocentesis.
item.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether molecular integrated non-invasive fetal exome sequencing (iNIFS), using clinical exome sequencing of maternal-plasma cell-free DNA, concords per pregnancy with paired amniocentesis.
METHOD: Prospective, blinded, single center, paired sample diagnostic accuracy study in 641 consecutive pregnancies referred for clinically indicated amniocentesis at 16-18 weeks. Plasma cell-free DNA underwent low-pass whole-genome sequencing for aneuploidies and CNVs and, after short-fragment enrichment, clinical exome sequencing within a parent fetus trio design. The reference standard comprised QF-PCR, karyotyping, array-comparative genomic hybridization and, where indicated, trio clinical exome sequencing on amniotic-fluid DNA.
RESULTS: iNIFS was reportable in 624/641 pregnancies (97.3%); 612 (95.5%) had complete paired data and formed the analysis population. The reference established a pathogenic or likely pathogenic finding in 107/612 (17.5%). NIPT gave 106 true positives, 503 true negatives, 2 discordant positives and 1 discordant negative: sensitivity 99.1% (95% CI 94.9-99.8), specificity 99.6% (98.6-99.9), PPV 98.1% (93.5-99.5), NPV 99.8% (98.9-100.0), agreement 99.5% and Cohen's κ 0.98. The discordant negative was a maternally inherited variant, the class for which distinguishing maternal from fetal contributions is most challenging.
CONCLUSION: Molecular iNIFS showed high concordance with paired amniocentesis across chromosomal, copy-number and monogenic findings, while retaining an explicit no call rate. Multicentre validation and invasive confirmation of positive findings remain necessary.

item.title: Localized hydrogel depots for CAR-T cell therapy in solid tumors: materials design, cellular fitness and translational deployment.
item.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is less effective in solid tumors than in selected hematologic malignancies because vascular, stromal, spatial, and immunosuppressive barriers restrict cell delivery and function. Local hydrogels and related biomaterials can convert a transient administration into a spatially organized depot, but their benefit depends on more than polymer identity. This review therefore combines a scenario-driven framework-depot versus bolus, intratumoral versus peritumoral placement, unresected versus postsurgical disease, and cell-loaded versus cell-free support-with a materials-centered analysis of formation, administration, time-dependent mechanics, architecture, degradation, biochemical presentation, and manufacturing. Direct evidence is distinguished from adjacent mechanistic evidence and design hypotheses. Across the available studies, the best-supported functions are improved delivered-cell recovery, regional persistence, controlled presentation of supportive cues, and enhanced antitumor activity in selected preclinical models. By contrast, universal material-property optima, clinically validated hydrogel-CAR-T products, and cryopreservation of a final cell-loaded depot have not been established. We define practical tests for gelation and device compatibility, productive egression, material-to-cell fitness, component attribution, and integrated-product safety. A materials-focused comparative table and a 30-study evidence map separate measured values from inferred mechanisms and identify where CAR-T cells were directly loaded, administered separately, manufactured in a matrix, or generated in situ. The resulting framework emphasizes that successful platforms must coordinate material behavior, CAR-T quality, anatomical placement, and clinical workflow rather than maximizing retention or chemical complexity alone.

item.title: Osteocyte-Derived Extracellular Vesicles: Bridging the Gap in Skeletal Physiology and Pathophysiology.
item.abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Osteocytes are the most abundant cells in bone and serve as central skeletal regulators. Recent findings from our and other groups demonstrate that beyond soluble mediators, osteocytes communicate by releasing extracellular vesicles (EVs). This review provides a systematic overview of osteocyte-derived EVs and highlights their importance in diagnostic and therapeutic innovation.
RECENT FINDINGS: Accumulating evidence has linked osteocyte mechanotransduction to EV biogenesis and secretion. Mechanically induced calcium oscillations and signaling pathways impact load-induced EV release. Under normal conditions, osteocyte-derived EVs contribute to local and systemic intercellular communication within experimental models, whereas their direct role in immune-microenvironment remodeling remains insufficiently defined. In pathological states, alterations in osteocyte EV release and cargo composition are associated with both benign diseases and malignancies. Engineered osteocyte-derived EVs and EV-inspired delivery systems are being investigated as cell-free therapeutic platforms for skeletal regeneration. Continued research in osteocyte-derived EVs will deepen understanding of bone communication networks and resolve the principal conceptual and technical challenges.

item.title: Lactobacillus brevis cell-free supernatant attenuates inflammation-associated gene expression and differentially modulates host defense-associated genes in DSS-stimulated HT-29 cells.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dysregulated Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling in intestinal epithelial cells contributes to persistent mucosal inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Although Lactobacillus brevis has demonstrated anti-inflammatory potential, the transcriptional effects of its secreted metabolites on inflammatory and host defense-associated components of epithelial innate immune signaling remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigated the effects of L. brevis cell-free supernatant (CFS) on TLR-associated gene expression in DSS-stimulated HT-29 cells.
METHODS: 1% DSS stimulated HT-29 human intestinal epithelial cells (inflammatory epithelial model) were treated with 50% L. brevis CFS (48 h) following viability assessment using MTT assay. Transcriptional profiling of 84 key genes involved in the TLR signaling pathway was performed using the RT² Profiler™ PCR Array. Differential gene expression was analyzed using the ΔΔCt method, followed by pathway-level mapping of the MyD88- and TRIF-dependent branches. Raw p-values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg FDR procedure.
RESULTS: Treatment with L. brevis CFS was associated with significant downregulation of multiple inflammation-associated genes, including TLR2, TLR4, MYD88, TIRAP, IRAK1, IRAK4, MAP3K7, NFKB1, IL1A, IL1B, IL6, IL12A, CCL2, and PTGS2. Host defense-associated genes exhibited a non-uniform transcriptional response. Components of the TRIF-dependent antiviral axis, including TLR3, TICAM1, TBK1, IRF3, and CXCL10, were downregulated, whereas TLR1, TLR10, TICAM2, and BTK were upregulated, and several other immune-response genes showed no significant change. These findings indicate differential modulation of TLR-associated transcription rather than uniform suppression of all examined immune-related genes.
CONCLUSIONS: L. brevis CFS attenuated the expression of multiple inflammation-associated genes and differentially modulated host defense-associated genes in DSS-stimulated HT-29 cells. This non-uniform transcriptional pattern indicates selective modulation of the TLR-associated gene network rather than indiscriminate suppression of all examined immune-related genes.
item.authors: Moghanlou, Rasouli, Asadi Lanjavani, et al.

item.title: A Diabetic Wound Microenvironment-Responsive HAMA-PBA/PVA Hydrogel for Localized Delivery of Netrin-1-Enriched Adipose-Derived Stem Cell-Derived Exosomes Promotes Diabetic Wound Healing through Immunomodulation and Angiogenesis.
item.abstract: Diabetic wounds are characterized by persistent inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, impaired angiogenesis, and poor local retention of therapeutic agents, all of which hinder effective repair. Here, we combined Netrin-1-enriched exosomes (NTN-Exos) from genetically modified adipose-derived stem cells with a photo-crosslinkable phenylboronic acid-modified hyaluronic acid methacryloyl/polyvinyl alcohol (HAMA-PBA/PVA) hydrogel to create a diabetic wound-responsive exosome-hydrogel system. NTN-Exos@Gel enabled prolonged local exosome retention owing to its favorable injectability, biocompatibility, and pH- and reactive oxygen species-responsive degradation and release behavior. In vitro, NTN-Exos reduced high-glucose-induced endothelial apoptosis and restored endothelial migration, proliferation, and tube-forming capacity. Additionally, NTN-Exos reduced inflammatory reactions and promoted macrophage polarization toward a reparative phenotype. NTN-Exos@Gel dramatically accelerated wound closure, improved blood perfusion, boosted neovascularization, improved re-epithelialization and collagen deposition, and decreased local inflammatory cytokine production in a diabetic full-thickness wound model. Mechanistically, transcriptome and protein analysis showed that the pro-angiogenic action of NTN-Exos was associated with altered Hippo signaling, which is typified by higher YAP/TAZ expression, decreased phosphorylation of LATS1 and YAP, and increased expression of CD146. These results suggest that NTN-Exos@Gel is a viable cell-free approach for the healing of diabetic wounds.

item.title: Redox-Active Nanoceria Integrated with Glucose Oxidase for Glucose-Triggered Metformin Release: Promising Nanocarrier for Managing Oxidative Stress and Hyperglycemia in Diabetes Pathophysiology.
item.abstract: Development of a glucose-responsive drug delivery platform remains a promising strategy for self-regulated treatment of diabetes mellitus. In the present study, we developed a multifunctional nanocarrier system for the glucose-sensitive delivery of metformin (Met) based upon amine-functionalized nanoceria (NC-NH2) coupled with glucose oxidase (GOx) and capped with dextran. Nanoceria's inherent ability to scavenge reactive oxygen species (ROS) was made possible by its nanozyme feature, and GOx converts glucose into gluconic acid, and thereby causing drug release in a glucose-responsive manner. Drug release was controlled by the dextran shell, which served as a biocompatible gatekeeper. Under hyperglycemic conditions, the synthesized nanocarrier (NC-GOx-Met-Dex) demonstrated regulated, glucose-triggered metformin release with little release at normoglycemic levels. NC-GOx-Met-Dex showed good structural stability under physiologically simulated circumstances, selective glucose-dependent drug release kinetics in cell-free, in vitro, and ex vivo systems, and promising cellular uptake in muscle cells without causing any cytotoxicity. NC-GOx-Met-Dex enhanced glucose uptake, glucose utilization and translocation of glucose transporter protein (GLUT4) compared to the metformin-alone-treated group in palmitic acid-treated (PA, 0.75 mM) muscle cells. Further in vivo studies showed that compared to metformin alone-treated group, the nanocarrier group showed remarkable glycemic management, improvement of insulin levels, and increased metformin bioavailability in muscle tissues in animal models of diabetes mellitus. Nevertheless, NC-GOx-Met-Dex gavaging to untreated animals did not cause any abnormal behavior or adverse effects, and levels of hepato-renal biomarkers, as well as blood cell profiling, were comparable to the untreated group. In general, this research provides a viable strategy for personalized diabetes therapy through the use of a dual and multifunctional nanosystem capable of responding to hyperglycemia while preventing oxidative stress.
